plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000046) on paint-by-number kits: Dan Robbins at the Palmer Paint Company in Detroit, the Leonardo numbered-sketch inspiration, owner Max Klein, early poor sales, Craft Master, critics, and a 2001 Smithsonian exhibition. Topic checked against every bank (no matches); sales stated only as millions. Ten new items, four aimed at hard (colon vs semicolon before a phrase, sentence-deletion effect, agreement past an along-with phrase, sentence placement). Plus E045-07 resubmitted as revision 2, unchanged, on its banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000045 (flag was an intended trap). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Painting by Number
passages.text:
[1] In the early 1950s, Dan Robbins, a commercial artist at the Palmer Paint Company in Detroit, was looking for a way to sell more of the company's paint. [2] He remembered reading that Leonardo da Vinci had sometimes numbered sections of a sketch so that his apprentices would know which colors to apply. [3] Robbins applied the same idea to {{1|a kit, it contained}} a board printed with a numbered outline and small pots of matching paint.

[4] The company's owner, Max Klein, was doubtful at first. [5] Early kits sold poorly, {{2|because}} store owners did not know where to display them. [6] Sales {{3|improved dramatically}} after a department store demonstration showed shoppers that anyone could finish a picture in a few evenings. [7] Within a few years, Palmer was selling millions of kits a year {{4|under the name Craft Master}}.

[8] Not everyone approved. [9] Critics complained that the kits turned painting into a mechanical {{5|task; following}} instructions rather than expressing ideas. [10] {{6|To them, a picture that came with its own instructions could not really be called art.}} [11] Robbins, however, argued that the kits, along with the simple instructions included in each box, {{7|was}} a first step toward painting for many people who had never held a brush.

[12] Today, paint-by-number pictures {{8|were}} sought by collectors, including some who once dismissed them. [13] In 2001 the Smithsonian Institution held an exhibition of the paintings, presenting them as a record of how ordinary Americans {{10|spent its}} leisure time in the years after World War II.

passages.title: A Pan with a Hole in the Middle

candidates.subskill: Comma splice repaired with a relative clause
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: a board printed with a numbered outline
candidates.explanation: "That contained" turns the second idea into a relative clause describing the kit, so the sentence has one main clause.

A.rationale: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

B.rationale: "And contained" makes Robbins, not the kit, the subject of "contained."

D.rationale: Without "that," the sentence has two main verbs with no connection.

hints: What did the kit contain, and how is that idea attached to the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for a comma splice or a misplaced subject.

candidates.remember: A comma cannot join two complete sentences; use a relative clause or a conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: store owners did not know where to display them
candidates.explanation: The second clause gives the reason the early kits sold poorly, so "because" is the logical connector.

B.rationale: The second clause explains the poor sales; it does not contrast with them.

C.rationale: "So" reverses cause and effect: the poor sales did not make store owners unsure where to display the kits.

D.rationale: "Unless" sets up a condition that makes no sense here.

hints: Which clause is the cause and which is the result?

strategy.explanation: Decide which event led to the other.

candidates.remember: Check the direction of cause and effect before choosing a connector.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: dramatically improved in a dramatic way

candidates.explanation: "Improved dramatically" states the idea once, with no repetition.

B.rationale: "Improved" and "got better" mean the same thing.

C.rationale: "Dramatically" and "in a dramatic way" repeat each other.

D.rationale: "Dramatically" and "greatly" are redundant, and the commas interrupt the sentence.

hints: Do any choices say the same thing twice?

strategy.explanation: Pick the shortest version that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: When choices mean the same thing, the shortest clear one is best.

candidates.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined portion (ending the sentence with a period after the word year). Should the underlined portion be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it explains why the kits began selling so much better than before.
choices.B: Kept, because it identifies the brand name under which the kits were sold.
choices.C: Deleted, because it repeats information that was already given earlier in the essay.
choices.D: Deleted, because it contradicts the earlier statement that the early kits sold poorly.

candidates.evidence: Within a few years, Palmer was selling millions of kits a year
candidates.explanation: The phrase adds a fact found nowhere else, the kits' brand name, so it should be kept.

A.rationale: The phrase names the brand; the reason for better sales is the demonstration in sentence 6.

C.rationale: The name Craft Master appears nowhere else in the essay.

D.rationale: Naming the brand does not contradict anything about early sales.

hints: What does the phrase add that the essay does not say elsewhere?

strategy.explanation: Decide what the phrase contributes, then check the reasons.

candidates.remember: A phrase worth keeping adds information the reader would otherwise lack.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The phrase after the underline explains what kind of task painting became. A colon after an independent clause can introduce such an explanation.

A.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "following instructions rather than expressing ideas" is a phrase.

B.rationale: This leaves "Following instructions rather than expressing ideas" as a sentence fragment.

C.rationale: "And" has nothing to join after the colon; the phrase is meant to explain "task."

hints: Is the part after the underline a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what can legally follow a semicolon.

candidates.remember: A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides; a colon can introduce an explanation.

candidates.stem: If the writer were to delete sentence 10, the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.A: evidence that the kits sold better after the critics began to write about them in magazines.
choices.B: a statement of Robbins's own view about whether the pictures counted as art.
choices.C: an explanation of why the critics did not consider the finished pictures to be real art.
choices.D: a detail showing that the kits came with instructions printed on the board itself.

candidates.evidence: To them, a picture that came with its own instructions
candidates.explanation: Sentence 10 spells out the critics' reasoning: a picture with its own instructions could not count as art. Deleting it removes that explanation.

A.rationale: The sentence says nothing about sales.

B.rationale: The sentence gives the critics' view ("To them"), not Robbins's.

D.rationale: The sentence mentions instructions only to explain the critics' objection.

hints: Whose view does sentence 10 give, and what does it add?

strategy.explanation: Identify the sentence's job in the paragraph.

candidates.remember: Ask what job the sentence does, not just what it mentions.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Robbins, however, argued that the kits
candidates.explanation: Within the clause, the subject is "the kits"; the phrase between commas is not part of the subject. A plural past-tense verb, "were," is needed.

A.rationale: The subject is the plural "kits"; the phrase "along with the simple instructions" does not change it, but "was" is singular.

C.rationale: "Is" is singular and present tense, but the subject is plural and the account is in the past.

D.rationale: "Has been" is singular and does not agree with "kits."

hints: What is the subject of the verb?

strategy.explanation: Cross out the phrase between the commas.

candidates.remember: Phrases like "along with" do not change the number of the subject.

candidates.subskill: Verb tense with a time marker
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Today" sets the time in the present, so the present-tense "are" is correct.

A.rationale: "Today" signals the present; "were" is past tense.

B.rationale: The past perfect does not fit a statement about the present.

C.rationale: The future perfect does not fit "Today."

strategy.explanation: Use the time word to choose the tense.

candidates.remember: Time words like "today" set the verb tense.

candidates.stem: For the sake of logic and cohesion, sentence 5 should be placed:
candidates.explanation: The paragraph moves in time order: the owner's doubts, early poor sales, improved sales after a demonstration, and finally millions sold. Sentence 5 belongs where it is.

B.rationale: Sentence 6 explains how sales improved, so the poor early sales must come before it.

C.rationale: Placing the early poor sales after the report of millions sold breaks the time order.

D.rationale: Sentence 4 introduces the owner's doubts, which the poor early sales then bear out; reversing them loses that link.

hints: What order do the events in paragraph 2 happen in?

strategy.explanation: Put the events in time order.

candidates.remember: Sentence order should follow time or logic; check what each sentence depends on.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to "ordinary Americans," which is plural, so the plural possessive "their" is correct.

A.rationale: "Its" is singular, but it refers to the plural "ordinary Americans."

B.rationale: "There" refers to a place, not possession.

strategy.explanation: Find the antecedent and match its number.

candidates.remember: A pronoun must match the number of the noun it refers to.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Baked in a Bundt pan, Helfrich watched as a ring of soft fudge formed inside her "Tunnel of Fudge" cake.
choices.C: Baked in a Bundt pan, there was a ring of soft fudge that formed inside her "Tunnel of Fudge" cake.
choices.D: Baked in a Bundt pan, her "Tunnel of Fudge" cake developed a ring of soft fudge inside.

candidates.explanation: An introductory modifier must be followed by the thing it describes. The cake was baked in the pan, so "her ... cake" must come right after the comma.

A.rationale: The modifier "Baked in a Bundt pan" attaches to the ring of fudge, which formed inside the cake, rather than to the cake itself.

B.rationale: Helfrich herself was not baked in a Bundt pan.

C.rationale: The modifier has nothing it can logically describe; "there" is not what was baked.

hints: What was baked in the pan?

strategy.explanation: Put the thing the modifier describes right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier describes the noun that comes right after it.
